Let $\zeta(a)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac1{m^a}$ (which converges because $a>1$).  
Pick any constant $C>\zeta(a)$; for concreteness set
$$C=1+\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac1{m^a}.$$

**Inductive construction.**  
Set $x_0=0$. Suppose $x_0,x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\in[-C,C]$ have already been chosen.  
To choose $x_n$, note that the condition $|x_n-x_k|\ge (n-k)^{-a}$ forbids $x_n$ from lying in the open interval
$$I_{n,k}=\left(x_k-\frac1{(n-k)^a},\;x_k+\frac1{(n-k)^a}\right),\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n-1.$$
The total length of these forbidden intervals is at most
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2\cdot\frac1{(n-k)^a}=2\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac1{m^a}<2\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac1{m^a}=2(C-1)<2C.$$
Since $[-C,C]$ has length $2C$, the union $\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}I_{n,k}$ cannot cover $[-C,C]$.  
Define $x_n$ to be any point in $[-C,C]\setminus\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}I_{n,k}$ (for definiteness, take the smallest such point).

**Verification.**
- *Boundedness:* By construction $|x_n|\le C$ for every $n\ge0$.
- *The inequality:* Let $i>j$ be any two distinct indices. When $x_i$ was chosen, it was selected outside $I_{i,j}$, so $|x_i-x_j|\ge (i-j)^{-a}$. Hence
$$|x_i-x_j|\cdot|i-j|^a\ge1.$$

Thus the sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ is bounded and satisfies the required condition for every pair $i\ne j$.
